_supersedes: user_prompt/v1 is FROZEN by PREREGISTRATION.md section 8 and is not edited. v2 adds `complexity` alongside the original `route`; both travel in one Jev call, so the marginal cost of the second question is near zero against ~278 tokens of fixed scaffolding.
_why_a_score_not_a_model_choice: With three tiers (haiku / sonnet / opus) a direct 'which model' question would bake one policy into the measurement: you could evaluate exactly that policy and no other. A 1-5 complexity score plus TWO thresholds partitions into three tiers, and lets every routing policy be evaluated offline from one set of rows -- including policies invented after collection ends. The day-0 probe also found the score question outperformed the choice question (FINDINGS 5.3).

_tier_mapping._comment: NOT part of the question. This is the POLICY applied in analysis, kept here so it is versioned alongside the question it consumes. Two thresholds, both to be selected by a rule on training data rather than memorised -- see JEV-17 and FINDINGS 4d.
_tier_mapping.rule: score <= tau_low -> haiku;  tau_low < score <= tau_high -> sonnet;  score > tau_high -> opus
_tier_mapping.escalate_on_low_confidence: If confidence < 0.5 OR needs_frontier >= tau_frontier, route UP one tier. tau_frontier is 0.65, NOT 0.5: on a 7-prompt check Jev's needs_frontier ran 0.47-0.50 on trivial and simple prompts and 0.70-0.78 on moderate and hard ones -- clean separation, but not at the default. At 0.5 it escalated 5 of 7 including a simple test-writing prompt, which would route nearly everything to opus and destroy the economics. This is the same ceiling-hugging inflation found on pre_bash.needs_review: Jev ranks well and calibrates badly. Like every other threshold here, 0.65 is a STARTING VALUE to be replaced by a rule selected on training data -- see JEV-17.
_tier_mapping.asymmetry: Misrouting easy->strong wastes money. Misrouting hard->weak burns turns, produces a wrong answer, and you pay for the rework AND the escalation. Thresholds must be conservative; this is a decision-curve question over the FN:FP cost ratio, not a Youden question.

complexity._comment: Ordered low to high. Anchors describe the WORK, never the model -- naming models in the anchors would leak the policy into the measurement and make the score unusable if the tier lineup changes.
anchors: Mechanical: a rename, a format, a lookup with one right answer
Localised: a single file, an obvious approach, nothing to weigh up
Ordinary engineering: several files, but the approach is already specified
Diagnosis: the cause is not stated and must be inferred from symptoms
Open-ended design: real trade-offs, no stated approach, consequences beyond this change

phrasings.a: How much reasoning does this request require?
phrasings.b: How hard is this to get right?
phrasings.c: How much would a weaker engineer struggle with this request?

needs_frontier._comment: A deliberate cross-check on the score, and the safety-critical half of the pair. The score is optimised for ranking; this is optimised for catching the one case that must not be downgraded. If the score says 2 and this says 0.9, that disagreement is the signal -- exactly the destructive/needs_review pairing that worked on pre_bash.

phrasings.a: Would a smaller, faster model plausibly get this wrong in a way the user would notice?
phrasings.b: Does this request need the strongest available model?
phrasings.c: Is there a real risk that a cheap model answers this confidently and incorrectly?

route._comment: Carried forward unchanged from v1 so the two versions remain comparable and the choice-type machinery (option-order sensitivity, categorical kappa) keeps being exercised.

options.explain: Explain existing code or a concept
options.shell: Run a command or perform an operational task
options.search: Find something in the codebase or externally
options.review: Assess the quality or correctness of existing work

phrasings.a: What kind of work is the user asking for?
phrasings.b: Which single category best describes this request?
phrasings.c: If you had to route this prompt to one specialist, which one?
